description:
Abraham Ortelius's map of Tartary, from the first edition of his atlas, the Theatrum orbis terrarum (Antwerp, 1570). It runs from the Volga to Japan and the edge of America, and its 40 engraved texts cite Marco Polo, Pliny and Hayton the Armenian. Several place the lost Ten Tribes of Israel in northern Asia.
Each numbered pin opens one of those texts: the Latin as engraved, the abbreviations written out, and an English translation. All of it was read from the scan by an AI model, Claude Opus 5.5, then compared with Marcel van den Broecke's published edition at orteliusmaps.com. Overall, 5.4% of characters differ once the published text's own errors are corrected, and 2.5% leaving out the one note hidden in the binding fold. The model also read 371 smaller place names; they are not pinned yet because their positions were not recorded.
Turn the sheet over for Ortelius's description of Tartary, printed on the back. This is the Boston Public Library copy, of the 1570 Latin issue B. HKUST's own copy of the map is in the collection without annotations.

text.original:
QVI Tartaros deſcribere velit, multas nationes deſcribat neceſſe eſt,
& eaſdem longè ab inuicem diſtantes. Nam Tartaria hodie ferè vo-
catur, quicquid terrarum ab Orientali Oceano, ſiue Mangico, poſi-
tum eſt inter Septentrionalem Oceanum & Meridionales regiones
Sinam, Indiæ partem extra Gangem, Sacos, Iaxartem (hodie Cheſel)
fluuium, mare Caſpium & Meotidis paludem; & ad Moſcos penè
Occidentem verſus: quia hæc omnia ferè occupauerunt Tartari, &
in iiſdem locis reſiderunt. Ita vt antiquorum ſcriptorum Sarmatiam
Aſiaticam, vtramque Scythiam, Sericamq́ue regionem (quæ fortaſ-
ſe hodie Cataio eſt) compræhendat. Horum nomen Anno ſalutis
M.CC.XII. primùm in Europa auditum eſt.
text.expanded: QVI Tartaros describere velit, multas nationes describat necesse est, & easdem longè ab inuicem distantes. Nam Tartaria hodie ferè vocatur, quicquid terrarum ab Orientali Oceano, siue Mangico, positum est inter Septentrionalem Oceanum & Meridionales regiones Sinam, Indiæ partem extra Gangem, Sacos, Iaxartem (hodie Chesel) fluuium, mare Caspium & Meotidis paludem; & ad Moscos penè Occidentem versus: quia hæc omnia ferè occupauerunt Tartari, & in iisdem locis residerunt. Ita vt antiquorum scriptorum Sarmatiam Asiaticam, vtramque Scythiam, Sericamq́ue regionem (quæ fortasse hodie Cataio est) compræhendat. Horum nomen Anno salutis M.CC.XII. primùm in Europa auditum est.
text.translation: Whoever would describe the Tartars must necessarily describe many nations, and these far distant from one another. For today Tartaria is generally the name for whatever land lies from the Eastern Ocean, or Mangic [Ocean], between the Northern Ocean and the southern regions (Sina, the part of India beyond the Ganges, the Saci, the river Iaxartes (today Chesel) [Syr Darya], the Caspian Sea and the Meotis marsh [Sea of Azov]), and toward the Mosci [Muscovites], almost to the west: because the Tartars have occupied nearly all these lands and have settled in those same places. So that it comprises the Asiatic Sarmatia of the ancient writers, both Scythias, and the Serican region (which is perhaps today Cataio [Cathay]). Their name was first heard in Europe in the year of salvation 1212.
text.commentary:

text.original:
In hordas diuiduntur,
quæ vox illis ſignificat conuentus, aut multitudo. Sed vt varias longè
lateq́ue diſtantes Prouincias inhabitant, ita neque in moribus aut vitæ
genere omnes conueniunt. Homines ſtatura quadrata, lata facie & obe
ſa, oculis contortis & concauis, ſola barba horridi, cetera raſi, corpore
valido, animo audaci; equis, aliisq́ue animalibus quoquo modo in-
teremptis ſuauiter veſcuntur, demptis porcis, à quibus abſtinent: ine-
diæ ſomniq́ue patientiſſimi: equitantibus porrò ſi fames ſitisq́ue illos
moleſtauerit, equis quibus inſident venas ſolent incidere, hauſtoq́ue
eorum ſanguine famem pellunt.
text.expanded: In hordas diuiduntur, quæ vox illis significat conuentus, aut multitudo. Sed vt varias longè lateq́ue distantes Prouincias inhabitant, ita neque in moribus aut vitæ genere omnes conueniunt. Homines statura quadrata, lata facie & obesa, oculis contortis & concauis, sola barba horridi, cetera rasi, corpore valido, animo audaci; equis, aliisq́ue animalibus quoquo modo interemptis suauiter vescuntur, demptis porcis, à quibus abstinent: inediæ somniq́ue patientissimi: equitantibus porrò si fames sitisq́ue illos molestauerit, equis quibus insident venas solent incidere, haustoq́ue eorum sanguine famem pellunt.
text.translation: They are divided into hordas, a word which among them signifies assemblies, or a multitude. But just as they inhabit various provinces lying far and wide apart, so neither do they all agree in customs or manner of life. They are men of square stature, with a broad and fat face, with twisted and hollow eyes, shaggy only in the beard, shaven everywhere else, strong of body, bold of spirit; they feed with relish on horses and other animals killed in any manner whatever, except pigs, from which they abstain: they are most enduring of hunger and of [want of] sleep: moreover, if hunger and thirst trouble them while they are riding, they are accustomed to cut open the veins of the horses on which they sit, and, having drunk their blood, they drive away hunger.

Et quoniam incertis vagantur ſedi-
bus, ſtellarum, imprimis verò Poli Arctici, quem ipſi ſua lingua Seles-
nikol, hoc eſt, ferreum clauum (teſte Sigiſmundo ab Herberſtein,) vo
cant, aſpectu, curſum ſuum dirigere ſolent. Vno in loco non diu com-
morantur, rati grauem eſſe infelicitatem diu in eodem loco hærere.
Iuſtitia apud illos nulla. Homines ſunt rapaciſſimi, nempe pauperri-

ſus.
text.expanded: Et quoniam incertis vagantur sedibus, stellarum, imprimis verò Poli Arctici, quem ipsi sua lingua Selesnikol, hoc est, ferreum clauum (teste Sigismundo ab Herberstein,) vocant, aspectu, cursum suum dirigere solent. Vno in loco non diu commorantur, rati grauem esse infelicitatem diu in eodem loco hærere. Iustitia apud illos nulla. Homines sunt rapacissimi, nempe pauperrimi; vt qui alienis semper inhiant. Auri & argenti apud eos nullus vsus.
text.translation: And since they wander with no fixed abodes, they are accustomed to direct their course by the sight of the stars, and above all of the Arctic Pole, which they themselves in their own language call Selesnikol, that is, the iron nail (on the testimony of Sigismundus ab Herberstein [Sigismund von Herberstein]). They do not stay long in one place, thinking it a grave misfortune to remain long in the same place. Among them there is no justice. They are most rapacious men, being indeed most poor; as men who are always gaping after the goods of others. Among them there is no use of gold and silver.

text.expanded: Tartaros, eorumq́ue mores & ritus accuratissimè descriptos habes apud Sigismundum ab Herberstein. Vide & Antonij Bonfinij commentaria Hungarica; Marcum Paulum Venetum, quem diu inter illos vixisse constat. De eorum origine lege Mathiam à Michou; Haythonum Armenum; Cælium Curionem in historia Sarracenica; & literas Iacobi Nauarchi Iesuitæ. De Tartaris habes etiam quædam non negligenda apud Nicephorum, libro. 18. capite 30. 47
text.translation: The Tartars, and their customs and rites, you have described most accurately in Sigismundus ab Herberstein. See also the Hungarian commentaries of Antonius Bonfinius [Antonio Bonfini]; M. Paulus Venetus [Marco Polo], who, it is established, lived among them for a long time. On their origin read Mathias à Michou [Maciej of Miechów]; Haythonus the Armenian [Hayton of Corycus]; Caelius Curio [Celio Secondo Curione] in the Saracen history; and the letters of Iacobus Nauarchus, Jesuit. On the Tartars you also have some things not to be neglected in Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 30. [Page number:] 47
